title: System-evolutionary view of RNA presence in living cells
summary: Our guiding question for this article was: How did RNA adjust its life when the RNA world era came to an end? RNA has its practical execution side in the whole-cell systems setup serving critical functions in metabolism, compartmentalization, and in the RNA-DNA-Protein network, coupling information handling and different events of macromolecule production into a self-sustaining loop. Aligning with current views of cooperation we find that RNA life is distributed across a population of information-bearing entities persisting by compatibility, with DNA serving as a long-term memory and proteins offering the catalytic reach. We suggest that the reproduction-survival axis, relevant to higher organisms, is also manifested by RNA in many forms, including RNA-primers, mRNAs, tRNAs, and rRNAs. Each of these have contrasting, highly adapted molecular phenotypes. Ultimately, we wish to emphasize the evolutionary narrative where RNA did not lose in exchange for DNA genes or otherwise. Ultimately, RNA just changed strategy and in its various forms has an active and critically important presence in all cells at all times.

title: An autoencoder outperforms two transformers on prediction of gene expression from chromatin accessibility
summary: Models that predict RNA abundance from chromatin accessibility are rarely compared under the same features, targets and metrics. We built one benchmark on 126,604 paired single-nucleus profiles from 19 human studies with a shared vocabulary of 50,000 peaks and 3,185 genes, ten 5x2 cross-validation folds and one scoring target, and compared seven implemented pipelines and two reference predictors across 70 trained runs; each pipeline keeps its own input normalisation and native training target. The scButterfly-B pipeline, built on dual variational autoencoders, outperformed every transformer pipeline, including an autoregressive Perceiver model (Omic Translator) and a support-free reformulation of Cisformer, on per-gene and within-cell Spearman correlation in all sixty paired fold comparisons, with 3.8 times shorter training. Transformer pipelines come within 0.02-0.04 on within-cell profile shape but lag by 0.10-0.24 on per-gene correlation. On two withheld cell types per-gene correlation is low; controls show the podocyte values are typical of within-type correlation for seen cell types of the same size, whereas Paneth values match a cell-agnostic shuffle for every Omic Translator arm. Within the transformer family, prespecified ablations show the Perceiver encoder was worth +0.0439 in within-donor per-gene correlation over full self-attention, a chromosome-aware genomic attention prior reduced it by 0.0096 (exact donor-level sign-flip test, Holm-adjusted p = 1.2e-4), and decoder output order had no detectable effect. A training-mean profile reaches 0.314 within-cell correlation with no input and a constant at the true expressed-gene positions reaches 0.996 per-gene correlation, so oracle-support protocols are reported only as diagnostics. Code, results and an audited release are provided.

title: Vagus nerve stimulation strengthens beta- and gamma-rate auditory steady-state responses in rat cortex
summary: Background: Gamma entrainment using sensory stimulation (GENUS) is under study as a treatment for neurological disease, but cortical engagement is variable. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) modulates cortical state and sound-evoked beta-gamma activity, suggesting that it may strengthen responses to rhythmic sensory input. Objective: To determine whether VNS strengthens auditory steady-state responses across beta and gamma rates and whether the effect depends on cortical region and sensory drive. Methods: Electrocorticography (ECoG) was recorded from core and belt auditory cortex, insular auditory field (IAF), and anterior insular cortex (AIC) in seven isoflurane-anesthetized rats before and 90 min after initiation of 30-Hz cervical VNS. Responses to 500-ms click trains at 20 and 40 Hz were quantified using inter-trial phase clustering (ITPC), event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP), and debiased weighted phase-lag index (WPLI). Results: VNS increased click-evoked P1-N1 amplitude. During 40-Hz trains, 40-Hz ITPC and ERSP increased only in auditory core. During 20-Hz trains, 20-Hz ITPC increased in core, belt, and IAF, whereas ERSP increased only in core; 40-Hz harmonic responses increased only in core. AIC showed no change. Within auditory cortex, WPLI increased selectively at frequencies present in each click train and not in the alpha band. Conclusions: VNS strengthened beta- and gamma-rate stimulus-locked responses in auditory-driven cortex without globally increasing synchrony. VNS may therefore enhance auditory cortical target engagement during GENUS, although effects on disease pathology or clinical outcomes remain untested.

title: A Multiscale Kinetic Model of DNA Damage Signalling and Repair under Combined Proton and Nanoparticle Exposure
summary: We present a multiscale kinetic framework for predicting the induction, processing, and biological consequences of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in AG1522 human fibroblasts exposed to combined proton and 15-nm GNP irradiation. The model connects proton dose and linear energy transfer (LET), perinuclear GNP localization, secondary-electron and reactive-species production, and Poisson--Gamma-distributed lesion induction. Initial DSBs are separated into simple and complex classes and coupled to an ATM--$γ$H2AX--53BP1 signalling cascade, cell-cycle-dependent allocation among canonical non-homologous end joining, homologous recombination, alternative end joining, and single-strand annealing, and class-specific repair fidelities. The model identifies the initial complex-lesion fraction and its slower resolution, rather than post-irradiation conversion of simple DSBs, as the principal determinants of persistent damage under high-LET, GNP-enhanced irradiation. The residual-DSB results provide strong internal out-of-sample validation of the kinetic component. However, the opposing biases in correct repair and misrepair reveal an inconsistency between the class-specific fidelities and the supplied integrated-fidelity endpoint. These repair-fate predictions should therefore be regarded as model-constrained estimates pending independent measurements of correct-end joining, mutation, chromosome aberrations, and clonogenic survival.

title: Learning Epidemic Threshold Equations from Simulation: REEBLRA, an Interpretable Bayesian Classification Framework for Reproduction Numbers
comment: 106 pages including Supplementary Information, 8 figures, 55 tables
summary: The basic reproduction number, $R_0$, is central to infectious-disease modelling, yet analytic expressions can be difficult to derive for high-dimensional, nonlinear, or structurally complex models. We introduce REEBLRA ($R_0$ Equation Estimation using Bayesian Logistic Regression Algorithm), an interpretable framework that learns explicit surrogate equations for epidemic thresholds from parameter--response data. Rather than directly regressing $R_0$, REEBLRA estimates $\Pr\{R_0(\boldsymbolθ)>c\}$ for parameter vector $\boldsymbolθ$ and threshold $c$. It provides a binary equation for classifying epidemic invasion ($R_0>1$) and successive threshold equations defining ordered brackets that approximate $R_0$, the expected number of secondary infections caused by a typical case in a fully susceptible population. The resulting equations support parameter screening, sensitivity interpretation, threshold classification, and exploratory analysis when analytic derivation is cumbersome. Bayesian logistic regression using standardized polynomial-like features and proper weakly informative priors yields regularized estimates, posterior uncertainty, and finite coefficients under complete or quasi-complete separation. We establish a mechanistic--surrogate concordance principle linking the full fitted-score gradient to the local gradient of $\log R_0$ under explicit regularity and tangency assumptions, allowing conditional interpretation of threshold directions. Across seven analytic-label benchmarks associated with ODE models, including a 15-compartment five-group SIR system, five-fold binary AUC was 0.999--1.000 and ordered-bracket accuracy was 0.951--0.998. REEBLRA complements rather than replaces mechanistic derivations, bridging simulation, machine learning, and reproduction-number analysis. An accompanying Shiny app supports implementation.

title: Bayesian Comparison of Covid Origins Hypotheses
summary: Applying standard Bayesian methods to the most reliably known unclassified facts about the Covid epidemic allows crude estimation of the odds for research-related vs. purely zoonotic origins. Here a broadly inclusive zoonotic hypothesis is compared with a rather specific subset of the research-related hypothesis defined by known prior work and grant proposals. The important observations are the type of virus, the city of the first outbreak, the lack of known prior hosts, the anomalous early pattern of evolution, and two specific features of the viral sequence. The resulting odds strongly favor research. The odds remain fairly strong under inclusion of uncertainties in prior odds.

title: Unlocking the Full Potential of Taylor Dispersion Analysis Through Advanced Detection
summary: Today, pharmaceutical sciences rely on a wide range of innovative therapeutics of varying sizes: nanoparticles, proteins, antibodies, and nanocarriers for drug delivery. Measuring their size is one of the crucial parameters in their characterization, to ensure drug safety, stability, and effectiveness. Over the past two decades, Taylor Dispersion Analysis has emerged as an important sizing method. Its scope of application is perfectly suited to the sizes of these therapeutics. By design, it can be coupled with a wide range of detectors, and extensive research has been conducted in this field. In this review, we will present an overview of the studies conducted, and discuss how the application drives the choice of one detector or another (size measurement, aggregation studies, interaction studies, and other analyses, performed in both simple biological buffers and in more complex media, particularly serum) and makes Taylor Dispersion Analysis a highly versatile tool.

title: When to retire: the cultural evolution of post-reproductive oblique teaching
comment: 53 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. SI Appendix (9 sections, 6 supplementary figures, 3 supplementary tables) is appended to the main text
summary: Teaching is ubiquitous across human societies. Instruction from parents to offspring is the most fundamental form of teaching, explained primarily through kin selection and inclusive fitness. Instruction to non-kin, known as oblique teaching, also plays a dominant role in modern societies, where teaching is often institutionalized. Nonetheless, it remains puzzling how or when oblique teaching can evolve. Here we address the evolution of oblique teaching by developing a mathematical model of stage-structured populations. Younger individuals engage in a useful activity, called hunting, and reproduce. At some point in life, they cease contributing directly to hunting and reproduction, and instead serve exclusively as teachers who increase the hunting expertise of the young. We refer to this transition in life stage as retirement, and we analyze the evolution of the retirement rate, and the resulting frequency of post-reproductive teachers, in a population subject to a global carrying capacity. We find that retirement and teaching can evolve without kinship or inclusive fitness, but only in populations above a threshold size. Unlike in classical adaptive dynamics, the evolutionarily stable retirement rates depend on the absolute population size of a mutant type upon introduction. In many regimes, evolution produces fewer teachers than would maximize the population's per-capita hunting returns or intrinsic birth rate. A mutant that differs only slightly from the resident type generally cannot invade from a minority, so teaching cannot emerge through gradual evolution. The mechanism we describe is therefore available to cultural evolution, where a distinct norm for retirement and elder care may be adopted by a sub-population simultaneously. Our account is thus tied closely to theories of cultural evolution, including the "information grandmother hypothesis" of Henrich and Henrich.

title: A Reverse-Gold Theorem: Positive-Data Identification by Substrate-Bounded Contrastive Learners
summary: Gold's theorem shows that no learner can identify an arbitrary language in a superfinite class from positive presentations alone. We prove a positive result of a different shape. Fix an innate \emph{recursive contrast operator} $R$ mapping any string to a finite set of structurally bounded perturbations of it, and a discriminative scorer of bounded capacity trained by InfoNCE-style contrastive estimation \citep{vandenoord2018,macollins2018} on self-generated perturbations. Under a faithfulness condition relating operator, scorer, and target, the trained scorer achieves \emph{PAC conditional identification} from positive data alone: with high probability it ranks all but an $\varepsilon$-fraction of positives above every out-of-language perturbation in their own orbit, with sample complexity polynomial in the capacity, the orbit size, the score bound, and $1/\varepsilon$. The negatives are constructed by the learner, not supplied by an oracle, and no global normalizing constant over strings is ever computed. The misranking bound follows from the geometry of the contrastive loss---per-example loss floors plus a definite loss increment under misranking---yielding an $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate, together with an explicit approximation gap that quantifies the cost of in-language (``colliding'') perturbations and vanishes for orbit-pure operators. The ranking guarantee lifts to a global membership classifier under a margin condition, and the same operator composed with the learned scorer is a normalization-free Metropolis--Hastings generator. We instantiate the hypotheses for substitutable context-free languages \citep{clarkeyraud2007} and the subregular classes \citep{heinz2010,hayashikamigaito2025}, and state an open conjecture locating the construction in the mildly context-sensitive hierarchy.

title: QUBO-Based Conformer Selection with Quantum-Classical Hybrid Optimization for Multiconformer Ligand Modeling
summary: A ligand can adopt multiple conformations within the same binding site, and these conformations can interact differently with the surrounding protein. Multiconformer modeling must therefore determine which candidate conformations to retain and what occupancies to assign to them. An established automated approach uses mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) with hard occupancy and conformer-count limits for this selection. Here, we reformulated conformer selection as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem with finite penalties and discrete occupancies. We solved the QUBO using a quantum-classical hybrid solver. We compared this workflow with the MIQP-based qFit-ligand workflow across 83 paired X-ray ligand entries using the same experimental inputs and the same qFit-ligand processing protocol. For each entry, both final models were evaluated against the same composite-omit map generated from the common input structure before the two workflows diverged. Quantum-qFit produced higher ligand-region real-space correlation coefficients (RSCC) in 62 entries 74.7% and lower occupancy-weighted torsional strain in 66 entries 79.5%. Similar directional trends remained in the 28 entries with matched final conformer counts. The molecular Electron Density for Individual Atoms score (EDIAm) decreased in most entries. This result shows that higher regional map agreement did not necessarily correspond to stronger atom-level density support. Overall, the results show that the conformer-selection formulation can change which ligand states are represented from the same experimental data and provide a QUBO framework for studying multiconformer ligand selection.

title: Bio-Inspired Auditory Processing: Coupling Parallel Resonate-and-Fire Dynamics with Ternary Recurrent Networks for Speech Recognition
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient inference through sparse, event-driven computation, yet remain constrained on continuous, context-dependent tasks such as automatic speech recognition (ASR). A key bottleneck is the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane decay erases information across pauses and phonetic boundaries while it must both extract features and retain long-range context. Inspired by cortical separation of nonlinear filtering and somatic integration, we introduce the Spiking Ternary GRU (stGRU): a ternary-weight gated recurrent unit performs temporal filtering, while downstream Resonate-and-Fire (RF) neurons generate the binary spike stream driving the next block's event pathway. This makes binary event transmission a native training constraint rather than a separate deployment-time activation quantization step; together with ternary weights, learned projections avoid dense floating-point matrix MACs. Trained end-to-end on LibriSpeech-960, Small, Medium, and Large stGRUs reach 8.09%, 7.04%, and $6.44 \pm 0.17\%$ WER on test-clean without an external language model. To our knowledge, these are the first matrix-MAC-free spiking networks without a learned ANN sequence decoder to achieve single-digit WER on LibriSpeech. The architecture also achieves 10.88% test CER on Aishell-1 (9.28% on dev) when trained from scratch. Internally, trained networks develop a depth-graded hierarchy: shallow layers act as fast acoustic filters, while deep layers form slower semantic integrators whose latent representations segregate into part-of-speech manifolds and word-level spike events. Deep-layer firing rates follow lognormal distributions with a sparsity gradient, mirroring hierarchical processing observed in human cortex in vivo. Our biologically grounded architecture combines competitive ASR with favorable modeled compute and memory cost.

title: Phenotype-structured nonlocal aggregation models I: signal production and response
summary: Individuals within a cellular or ecological population can exhibit substantial variation in their traits or phenotype. Such heterogeneity can fundamentally alter population-level behaviour, including the ability to aggregate and form spatial patterns. We investigate these effects by extending nonlocal aggregation models, widely used to model cell--cell adhesion and collective animal movement, to incorporate phenotype structure. We characterise how heterogeneity and switching between phenotypes affect whether patterns form, how phenotypes are distributed within them, and whether they are stationary or exhibit spatio-temporal oscillations. We show that pattern formation is promoted when phenotypes that produce stronger interaction signals also respond more strongly to them, whereas specialisation towards either signal production or response inhibits pattern formation. Increasing rates of switching between phenotypes dampen these effects. Heterogeneity can also enable weakly interacting, and even repulsive, individuals to pattern as part of the collective. Furthermore, movement in phenotype and physical space can interact to restructure patterns and generate spatio-temporal oscillations. A further key message of this study is the value of considering both discrete $N$-phenotype and continuous phenotype formulations. We develop both in parallel, demonstrating formal correspondences, but also advantages to each framework in terms of mathematical analyses and interpretability.
